deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is a draft of the historical part (Lagrange, Fourier, Cauchy, Dirichlet) of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (1854, publ. 1867). The page is prose. It contains one implicit mathematical idea (Lagrange's finite formula), one mathematical critique (of Cauchy), and historical claims.

(1) Lagrange's formula (continued from the previous page). The formula is
 y(x) = sum_{k=1}^n a_k sin(k pi x).
It is to take prescribed values Y_j at the nodes X_j = j/(n+1), j = 1..n. With the integral read as a sum, Lagrange's '2∫Y sin kXπ dX' means
 a_k = (2/(n+1)) sum_{j=1}^n Y_j sin(k pi j/(n+1)).
[My filling] This rests on the discrete orthogonality
 sum_{j=1}^n sin(k pi j/(n+1)) sin(l pi j/(n+1)) = ((n+1)/2) delta_{kl} for 1 <= k, l <= n.
Riemann's point is that if n -> infinity, the Riemann sum (1/(n+1)) sum_j becomes ∫_0^1. That gives the Fourier sine coefficients a_k = 2∫_0^1 f(X) sin(k pi X) dX, i.e. 'the Fourier result'. Lagrange did not take this step. Riemann's reasons:
- Lagrange held that arbitrary functions cannot be expressed by a formula.
- He held that trigonometric series represent only analytically given periodic functions.
- The Euler–d'Alembert dispute led him to finish the discrete n-mass vibrating string first and only then pass to the limit.

(2) Fourier. Fourier recognised the nature of the series correctly, and they were used widely in mathematical physics. Convergence was checked case by case when the coefficients were known in closed form, but a general proof came only later. In the right column there is a stray note: 'Der Beweis findet sich in der Inauguraldissertation des Verfassers' (the proof is in the author's inaugural dissertation).

(3) Cauchy's proof of 27 Feb 1826 is insufficient, as Dirichlet showed.
- Cauchy's hypothesis: f(x+iy) stays finite for every y.
- Riemann's objection: such a function (entire, periodic, bounded) must be constant. [Mine: Liouville's theorem, if 'finite' means uniformly bounded.]
- Riemann's weaker sufficient hypothesis: there is a function phi(x+iy), finite for all y > 0, whose real part tends to the given f(x) as y -> 0.
- He says this proposition is true, and that granting it, Cauchy's route works.
- Conversely, it follows from the Fourier series. [Mine] Take phi(z) = A_0/2 + sum_n (a_n - i b_n) e^{inz}, with z = x + iy and y > 0. Then
 Re phi(x+i0) = A_0/2 + sum (a_n cos nx + b_n sin nx),
and for y > 0 the series converges absolutely, damped by e^{-ny}.
- The dissertation note plausibly supports 'der in der That richtig ist': existence of such a phi with prescribed boundary real part is the Dirichlet-principle boundary-value theorem in Riemann's 1851 dissertation.

(4) Dirichlet, Crelle vol. 4 (Jan. 1829), proved convergence to f under these conditions:
- f has finitely many discontinuities and infinities;
- f has finitely many maxima and minima;
- f is integrable.
The case of infinities is handled in a later paper (Dove's Repertorium, 1837). This gave a firm foundation to analysis used throughout mathematical physics.
errors: 'Eine solche Function müsste nothwendig gleich einer constanten Grösse sein' holds only if 'finite for every y' means bounded on the whole plane (Liouville). Pointwise finiteness on each line is not enough: cos(x+iy) is finite for each fixed y but not constant. Riemann's 'endlich' is ambiguous here; the published text keeps the same phrasing.

In the weaker condition, 'finite for all positive y' cannot mean uniform boundedness up to y = 0. The harmonic conjugate of a bounded (even continuous) f can be unbounded as y -> 0. Pointwise finiteness for y > 0 is what the Fourier construction guarantees.

The phrase 'von der trigonometrischen Reihe glaubte er, dass sie jede analytisch gegebene periodische Function darstellen könne' is attributed to Lagrange somewhat loosely; it is a historical judgement, not a mathematical error.
No computational errors; the page has no explicit calculations.

results.what: Lagrange's finite sine-interpolation formula, and the observation that its n -> infinity limit gives the Fourier sine coefficients
results.modern_name: Discrete sine transform / trigonometric interpolation; Riemann-sum limit to Fourier coefficients
results.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1759–62); historical analysis in Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 1854/1867

results.what: Critique of Cauchy's 1826 convergence proof: a bounded entire periodic function is constant
results.modern_name: Liouville's theorem applied to Cauchy's hypothesis
results.usually_credited_to: Liouville/Cauchy 1844; the critique appears in Riemann's published Habilitationsschrift

results.what: Weaker sufficient condition: a function holomorphic for y > 0 whose real part has boundary value f; equivalence with Fourier representation
results.modern_name: Boundary values of holomorphic functions in the half-plane (Abel–Poisson summation, conjugate series)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (published 1867 Habilitationsschrift); later Fatou and others for rigorous boundary theory

results.what: Marginal reference to the inaugural dissertation as the source of the needed existence proof

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a draft of the published historical section of the 1854 Habilitationsschrift, and the wording is nearly identical to the printed text. The only unpublished detail is the marginal note linking the 'true' proposition about phi(x+iy) to his own dissertation, which is a minor bibliographic point.

checkable.asserts: Discrete orthogonality of sin(k pi j/(n+1)) underlying Lagrange's interpolation coefficients (n=6)

checkable.asserts: Lagrange's finite sine sum takes the prescribed values Y_m at X = m/(n+1) (expect list of zeros)
Real part of (a_n - i b_n) e^{in z} is e^{-ny}(a_n cos nx + b_n sin nx), so phi has real boundary value given by the Fourier series (expect 0)
cos(x+iy) is finite for every fixed y but unbounded as y grows, illustrating that 'finite for each y' needs to mean uniformly bounded for the constancy claim (expect 0)

transcription_corrections: Right column, bottom line: 'Der Beweis findet sich in der Inauguraldissertation des Verfassers.' This is a separate marginal/footnote line, apparently attached to the proposition about phi(x+iy), not to the Fourier paragraph.
'unzureichend[?]': the image shows 'durchaus ungenügend' struck through; the published text reads 'unzureichend', consistent with the replacement.
'Sich bei ihm' should be lower case, continuing the sentence: '…, dass sich bei ihm im Voraus eine bestimmte Ansicht … gebildet hatte'. The 'Voraus' insertion was moved.
'Es reicht[?] hin' is correct ('Es reicht hin'), matching the published text.
Insertion 'deren reeller Theil' belongs after 'welche … für alle positiven Werthe von y endlich ist und', i.e. 'deren reeller Theil für y=0 der gegebenen periodischen Function fx gleich wird'.

The final line is very uncertain. The published text ends the paragraph differently ('einer grossen Menge wichtiger analytischer Untersuchungen eine feste Grundlage gegeben'); the draft's last words are illegible here.
